THE WAR. THE FALL Or AHDAHAN.

The military event of the week seeml to be the fall of Ardahan. The preparations for crossing the Danube are being made with such secrecy that conjecture is wholly at fault into the eeleoted point of operations. The Daily Papers, as usual, abound with surmises suds' sculations as to the probable course of howilities. he military 0070. mandrel with the Mission and Turkish...ma- meats are equally jealous of the communi• cations of the newspaper correspondents permitted to accompany thereepective armies. Any revehtion as to their play of campaign would olearly be followed by OZIIIIISiOn, and therefore the newspaper letters from the seat of war are marked by extrao dinary reticence and discretion. This state of things renders it almost idle to deal with mere rumour, or indeed anything but with accomplished facts. Th • fall of Ardahan belonging to the latter category may therefore be usefully referred

to. Referring to this event, the Timn corms- pendent at Vienna dating his communication on Tuesday thus estimates its value and Ii gnificance:—“The fall of Ardahan, besides securing to the Russians their position before Ears, opens out a new line of operations either against the latter place or against &sermon. The event seems to have aroused the Turkish Government to a dim come:ions. noes of the danger threatening in that quer. ter, and in a Council of Ministers held the ' dey before yesterday it was determined to send all the reinforcetuen.s, which are still arriving at Constanbnople to be arm.d and fitted out, to Belo= and Erseroum. In I doing this, how over, the military authorities , in Constantinople eeem to overlook the fact that these troops, in making their way to Ears or lii mourn, would have to break through the Russian division barring the way at Tehuruk Cu. Indeed the advance of the Russian* against Ratoum does sot seem to have been undertaken so much with the view of taking that piece—which, defended se it is by the Turkish fleet and by the an.. tre obruents on the heights, could not be done easily—as with toe aim of locking up there 54 battalions of Turks, and preventing them or any other reintomments from get- ting by the Tahuruk Su line to Etheroum, or the positions taken up in front of this place." The Turkiso, Telegraph reluct- antly admits the fall of Ardahan, but insists that it was defended by the Turks with great gallantry. The correspondent states that the Turkish tro,ps were greatly out-num- bered, the Russians having massed 50,000 men for the assault, while the Ottoman Lithe did not exceed 11,000. The writer proceeds to measure the value of this exploit of the Russian arms, which the "wisest heads" amongst the Turks ''deem the poseible turn- ing point of the war" He says The fall of Ardahan no doubt will prove a great d vantage to the Russian amis, eine% by imp- . turing this position they clear their front, and can carry out their plans upon bars and Eizeroam. I should misrepresent the manly courage and selbreliance.which are reported to me from the fields of battle, and which I myself witness here among patriotic o:Atlan- tis, if I said that the Turks are at all in. dined to despair because of this disaster. But I must none the less deface to you that . . .

-e-w-ise—e—t -heads look upon the present time as the p wade turning point of the war." Later news add that the delisted turkiah soldiery flying from Ardahin were subse- quently defeated by the Russians in • moan. tam pass near Kart We have spoken of the taking of Ards. han as the event of the week. It is not certain, however, if the declaration of owaimian independence doe, not transcend it even in the matter of military importance. It is however, and besides, an affair of much relitical importance. Roumania has already fared war against Turkey, and its Prince expresses a hope that Roumanian indepen- dence is irrevocable, and will be recognised by the Powers as "constituting itself a guarantee for the peace of toe Danube." Of the immediate consequence of this action of Roumania the Time, says--“A. few months ago a declaration of Roumanian indepen- dence would have seemed like the letting loose of mighty waters, and our own Govern- ment would have been urged to take vigor ous measures to stop the deluge. But everybody can now see how very slight is the change compared with many other pos- sibilities. A Roumania bound to the Porte by the tie of a tribute which it did not pay was not separated from independence by a very wide gulf, and, now that the abyss has been filed by Parliamentary votes and a speech from the Prince, all oi us confess that to prevent the change was no business of ours. If Austria is satitlied, we have no reason to complain." In a summary of the "situation," and a forecast of what is im- pending, the Daily New, declares that "forces are gathei lug for a ark beside which all that has been done in A sia or on the Danube will seem the merest child's play. he Turkish superiority on the Black Sea may suddenly come to an end; the fighting on the Danube will begin, and we may hope tor results which will clear up the situation and cusp Ale men's minds to peace," Every consideration of humanity must inspire the wish that this terrible European explosion shall be short, sharp, and decisive.

div.p: PRESIDENT MACMAROWS COUP

A great political crisis has arrived in France, ! a crisis of such vast moment that the porton- • tons war cloud that ie bursting over Eastern Europe, scarcely suffices to obscure it. The Prime Minister and his Cabinet have re- signed office, or to speak with more exact- ness. have ilO.ll dismissed by the Marshal , Presides • MaeMahon. The Marshal has dons this in the teeth of the fact that the de- posed ministry were supported in the as- sembly by great majorities, and were acting in accordance with the existing constitution. The French nation is once more confronted , with the apparently intractable problem. how to reconcile a military dictatorship with the natural action of parliamentary institu- tion. A new Cabinet has been conetituted which is rightly described as a practical de claratien of war against the Republican majority in the Chamber of Deputies. The moment oboe n by the new Muter of Legions to plunge France into unknown and incalcul- able difficulties, is one when the country was recovering ins marvellous manner from the huge burden of the German indemnity, and had entered on a new career of commercial and inane rial prosperity. France, by its moderation and its freedom from political passion, its respect for opponents, and its abnegation in the matter el foreign compli- cations had become the wonder of Europe. It is impossible to deny that this astonishing change in thetemper and condition of France had grown up under the parliamentary in- stitutions embodied inn Chamber of Depu- ties and governed by the spirit of minim° ml responsibility The master of the Fri Doh as-sty has cheaen to put an end to all this, and to dismiss the Prime Minister of France and his Cabinet, with less courtesy than he would dismiss hie butler or the valet who ' brushes his regimentals. Marshal Mac. Mahon has abruptly reminded France that a soldier both reigns and governs, and that the drum head is practically the chief tribunal which regulates the rights of Frew% citizenship. It would have been wonderful however, if Fraser, having profited so largely by the calm ensured to it by parliamentary institu- tions, should surrender in a moment to the rule of the bayone', all that it had conquered in ita brief season of benedeent peace, The Parliament of France hail already adopted a resolution, by a majority of 335 against 15$ Mae, witch anat. the prioelple of pull&

mentary Gov rnment against the ominous , greesion of the Marshal Preeident, The kaeolution states that the House will , oenly place confidence in • Cabinet which is free in its action and resolved to govern according to liepublioan principles. The resolution was explained by M. Gamboa& in a speech which was much applauded. M. Gambetta pointed out that at a moment when no conflict had oc- curred, and when no vote had been passed placing the Ministry in a minority, the nation had suddenly learnt that Marshal Mach! ahon had written a letter necessitating M. Simon's resignation. M. Gamboa* denied that the President of the Republic had a responsibility over and above that of the Ministry. Those who told him so were his enemies, and were leading him to his ruin. He could not during his militaryeareer have studied politics The Chamber must re- call him to Mena. t obeervanoe of the Constitu - ties, and divert i,im from perilous counsels. The marshal ie thus in direct antagonism with—not alone the Ministry which he has deposed—but with the Parliament of France. One can realise the monstrous character of the political situation, by supposing that Lord Beaconsfield, or Mr. Gladstone, heving the immense support of a parliamentary majority of two hundred in the House of °ominous, were suddenly dismissed from Aloe by the Queen, and the representative of a small minority installed in their places ['hose who remember the story of the first Reform Bill in England (a story which has lately been so admirably re-told in these columns), can renal the scenes of agitation which convulsed the Empire, when the Monarch became the accomplice of a ocurupt parliamentary minority, in withstanding , the juet domande of the people of I rigla .d for political representation. The Ministry , and the corrupt minority were swept away by the mere breath of popular indignation, , and if the Monarchy was saved, it was only because the Monarchy consented to occupy the constitutional position which made the Ministry and not the Sovereign responsible to Parliament. It would be a grave insult to France to suppose, that with her recent precious tuperience, she will abdicate her high constitutional position and prostrate herself before a military dictator, who is him- self the conscious or unconscious creature of mixerable and obsolete dynastic ambition,. France has shown herself marvellously ca- pable of political forgiveness, but it must be doubted if she can ever pardon a Sedan. . .

- The mention of Sedan necessarily presses on one's attention the pregnant circumstance that all organic conflict at home must necee• airily vibrate through all the foreign rela- tions of a state which is the scene of it. It is impossible to speak of the condition of France without at the same m oneut think- ing also of Germany. Political observers, who speak with authority, already interpret the action of the President as a menses, more or less veiled, to Berlin. A correepon- dentin thatcapital, portentouslyremarkethat "It is an exinedingly hazardous experiment for the Hight at %. meanies to begin such a movement pending the adoption of imp irtant military measures by the German Govern- ment, and this opinion is publicly expressed with very little reserve." And yet it is im- possible to believe that the soldier-President of the Republic can have offered a deliberate and gratuitous defiance to Germany. Mar- shals of France may plan battles, more or less suocessful, but they have hardly ever given a statesman to their country. The masters of artillery are rarely political reit- loners. Marshal Mai:Mahon may not want to march on Berlin, but he appears to be provoking in France a political anarchy, which may be equally disastr u Nations may well exclaim. "The Lord deliver us from the men of War "
